title: Is Windows Movie Maker Still Available in 2026?
body:
Windows Movie Maker is not available from Microsoft and has not been since January 10, 2017, when every Windows Essentials 2012 installer was withdrawn. Old copies still install on Windows 10 and Windows 11 but get no patches or codec updates, and the official replacement is Clipchamp, which ships free on Windows 11 and exports up to 1080p without a watermark.

Quick facts
Launched
September 14, 2000, with Windows Me
Company
Microsoft
Final version
Movie Maker 2012, build 16.4.3528.0331, April 18, 2014
Status today
Discontinued January 10, 2017; no official download since
Price today
Replacement Clipchamp is free to 1080p; single paid plan reported at $11.99 a month

Why did Microsoft stop bundling a free video editor?

Windows Movie Maker shipped on September 14, 2000, inside Windows Me. That first release was thin: it saved to Microsoft's own ASF format and offered a short list of transitions and effects.

Windows XP carried a much stronger version from 2001, and a minor update, version 2.1, went out inside Service Pack 2. That is the release most Americans actually remember, with the storyboard strip along the bottom, the free effects and the fade to black.

The Windows Vista edition reported version 6.0 and added capture from HDV camcorders. Then Microsoft unbundled the program. Windows 7 shipped without Movie Maker, without Photo Gallery and without Windows Mail, so getting the editor back meant downloading the separate Windows Live Essentials suite.

The last packaged release was Windows Essentials 2012, and the final Movie Maker build, 16.4.3528.0331, arrived on April 18, 2014. Microsoft never charged a cent for any of it. Movie Maker was free for its entire 17-year life, which is exactly why its removal caught so many people flat.

Is Windows Movie Maker still available to download in 2026?

Not from Microsoft, and it has not been since January 10, 2017. That is the day the whole Windows Essentials 2012 suite reached end of support, and the installers came down with it.

Microsoft has not softened the wording in the nine years since. The suite is no longer offered for download, its support page says, but "already installed applications will continue to work as they do today."

That second clause is why the program never quite died. Copies already on a hard drive kept running, and they still run.

Microsoft also warns about the sites that moved into the gap. "Any websites offering free downloads of Windows Movie Maker are not offering sanctioned Microsoft products," the same page states, adding that those products may carry viruses or hidden costs.

Installers do survive on the Internet Archive, including the Windows Essentials 2012 bundle. Archived is not the same as audited, and an unsigned legacy installer from a community upload deserves a virus scan and a machine you can afford to rebuild.

Does Movie Maker still run on Windows 11?

Usually, with one step first. Movie Maker 2012 is a small 32-bit application that needs .NET Framework 3.5, which Windows 11 does not turn on by default. Walkthroughs published in 2026 all describe the same sequence: enable .NET 3.5, run the Essentials installer, and pick Movie Maker alone from the program list.

What the editor does not get is maintenance. Microsoft has shipped no security patch, no bug fix and no codec update since January 2017, and the company's own notice is blunt about the trade: there is "an increased security risk associated with use of unsupported products past their end of support date."

Codecs are the practical wall. Movie Maker handles what camcorders recorded in 2008 and stumbles on what phones record now: HEVC, variable frame rate footage, 10-bit color. Newer files can fail the render or corrupt it quietly.

Old projects are the other reason people hunt for it. Movie Maker saved edits as .MSWMM and .WLMP project files rather than finished video, so reopening a 2009 family slideshow means finding a working copy of the program that made it. Exported WMV and MP4 files still play anywhere, and the camcorder tapes behind those projects need a deck and a capture device before any editor can touch them.

How did a fake Movie Maker become a top global threat?

People kept searching for the installer, and in 2017 somebody monetized the gap. A site called windows-movie-maker.org climbed to the top of Google for the searches "Movie Maker" and "Windows Movie Maker," and reached the first page of Bing.

What it handed over was a working copy of Microsoft's free editor with a nag screen bolted on. Saving a file triggered a demand for $29.95 to unlock the full version, presented as a 25 percent discount on the operators' own payment page.

ESET logged the file as Win32/Hoax.MovieMaker and blocked the site. "Scammers have been surprisingly successful at distributing a modified version of Windows Movie Maker that aims to collect money from unaware users," the company wrote on WeLiveSecurity in November 2017. On November 5, 2017, the file ranked as the third most detected threat in ESET's worldwide telemetry.

The episode is the clearest measure of the demand Microsoft walked away from. A discontinued free program still pulled enough search traffic to push a scam into the global top three. Retiring free bundled software is a Microsoft habit, as anyone who watched Encarta go dark already knows.

What replaced Windows Movie Maker on Windows 11?

Microsoft's first answer was built in-house. Story Remix became the Video Editor inside the Photos app on Windows 10, a lighter tool with fewer manual controls than Movie Maker had.

The second answer was a purchase. Microsoft announced the acquisition of Clipchamp, a browser-based editor, on September 7, 2021, and Clipchamp shipped as a preloaded Windows 11 app in an Insider Preview build in March 2022.

In September 2023, the rebuilt Photos app dropped its own Video Editor and pointed people at Clipchamp instead. The older tool survives inside Photos Legacy, which Microsoft still lists in the Microsoft Store for anyone who wants the Windows 10 editor back.

Windows 10 reached end of support on October 14, 2025, which moved the last large group of Movie Maker holdouts onto Windows 11 or onto a machine with no patches.

Clipchamp has taken losses of its own. Microsoft retired the Clipchamp app for iOS on June 9, 2026, warning that projects left unexported could be deleted, and there has never been an Android version. Most users "prefer editing their video projects on our web and desktop applications," the support notice said.

Is the 2026 replacement actually free?

Mostly, and more generously than the free tier of most editors. Clipchamp exports up to 1080p on the free plan, with no standard watermark and no limit on how many videos you finish.

Above that line the structure changed. Clipchamp folded three paid tiers into a single plan, which Thurrott.com reported at $11.99 a month, and Clipchamp's pricing page now lists premium features as included with Microsoft 365 Personal and Family. 4K UHD export, premium stock media and the brand kit all sit on the paid side.

The wall is assets more than resolution. Drop a single premium stock clip, effect or music track into a project and the export is blocked until you either pay or pull the asset back out.

Set against Movie Maker's flat zero, that is the real then-versus-now shift. In 2000 the operating system was the thing you paid for and the editor came along for free. In 2026 the editor is free, the machine arrives with it installed, and the money has moved to stock footage and 4K output. Software that outlives its owner without a price tag, the way Winamp has, is now the exception.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I download Windows Movie Maker in 2026?

Not from Microsoft. Microsoft removed every Windows Essentials 2012 installer, Windows Movie Maker included, on January 10, 2017, and has never restored the download. Copies preserved on the Internet Archive still install on Windows 10 and Windows 11 once .NET Framework 3.5 is enabled, but they get no patches, and any site charging for the program is selling something Microsoft gave away free.

When did Windows Movie Maker stop being supported?

January 10, 2017. That is the date the whole Windows Essentials 2012 suite reached end of support, covering Windows Movie Maker, Windows Photo Gallery, Windows Live Mail and Windows Live Writer. The final Windows Movie Maker build, 16.4.3528.0331, had shipped almost three years earlier on April 18, 2014, and nothing has been released since.

What is the free replacement for Windows Movie Maker?

Clipchamp, which Microsoft bought on September 7, 2021 and preloaded on Windows 11 from March 2022. Its free plan exports up to 1080p with no standard watermark, while 4K export and premium stock come with a Microsoft 365 Personal or Family subscription or the single paid plan reported at $11.99 a month. The Windows 10 Video Editor that first replaced Windows Movie Maker is still reachable through the Photos Legacy app in the Microsoft Store.
